documents.title: Policy 100-022: Howard University Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy
documents.summary: Howard's university-wide AI policy (effective April 2026), owned by the Provost, applies to all community members. It sets general requirements (verify outputs, disclose when required, keep confidential data, PII and university data out of AI systems and out of model training), a teaching-and-learning section that has faculty set and communicate course AI rules and students ask when guidance is missing, plus sections on research, external AI partnerships and contracts, and work-related use, with annual review and disciplinary sanctions.

documents.title: Initial Howard University Guidelines for use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: The Provost's initial (2023) guidance on generative AI, framed by Howard's core values. It stresses bias against the African Diaspora, privacy, AI literacy and transparency, user responsibility for verifying AI output, and asks schools, departments and faculty to write discipline-specific policies with clear penalties. It treats undisclosed, unpermitted AI-created work as an academic-integrity concern while affirming students' right to defend themselves, and encourages responsible exploration.

units.policy: Generative AI is often conflated with Artificial General Intelligence (an autonomous, sentient intelligence), but it is not that.

units.policy: Generative AI refers to computer systems that produce forms of human expression such as written summaries, images, videos, music, or vocal mimicry.

units.policy: Generative AI continues a history of technological aids already familiar through word-processing spelling and grammar checkers and other automated guides in everyday technologies.

units.policy: Values and guidelines for AI are needed because writing and voice production remain important modes of critical, artistic, and sense-based learning vital to understanding and cognitive development.

units.policy: Tools such as ChatGPT represent a concerted shift in learning practices and definitions of integrity and require informed engagement.

units.policy: AI models and other content-generating tools fail to grasp the diverse nuances of human opinion, thought, and language, especially within the African Diaspora.

units.policy: AI technologies frequently echo dominant viewpoints of certain groups, spread misinformation, or generate inaccurate information as facts.

documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning & Assessment (CETLA), Office of the Provost
documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Teaching & Learning
documents.summary: CETLA's teaching-center page supplementing Policy 100-022. It restates the policy's definitions and lists responsibilities for faculty (communicate course AI rules, align with learning objectives, protect records), students (follow course rules, disclose when required, ask when guidance is missing, own their work) and all users (verify, protect data). It offers a three-level syllabus scheme (Disallowed, Restricted, Unrestricted) with sample language, recommended syllabus elements, a responsible-AI checklist, a tool overview including GitHub Copilot, and faculty-development resources.
